title: Joshua 19:1–9
context: With the tabernacle set up at Shiloh, Joshua casts lots for the seven tribes that had not yet received their inheritance (Joshua 18:1–10), and the second lot falls to Simeon. Simeon receives no separate territory but a group of towns within Judah’s large portion, because Judah’s share was too much for them. Many readers connect this arrangement with Jacob’s word that Simeon would be scattered in Israel (Genesis 49:7), and several of the same towns appear in Judah’s list (Joshua 15) and in Simeon’s list in 1 Chronicles 4:28–33. Arminian and Reformed readers commonly treat this town list as shared ground: the land is God’s gift distributed by lot, his promises reach even the smaller tribes, and tribal identity is preserved within the larger people. Many of these places cannot be located with certainty, and no theological disagreement turns on the list.

verses.text: The second lot came out for Simeon, even for the tribe of the children of Simeon according to their families. Their inheritance was in the middle of the inheritance of the children of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Simeon’s lot comes out second, showing that every tribe, however small, receives a place by God’s ordering. The inheritance inside Judah’s territory keeps Simeon within the people while giving it a real share.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the lot as God’s way of assigning inheritance, in keeping with the saying that every decision of the lot is from the LORD (Proverbs 16:33). Both traditions commonly read the placement within Judah as a gracious provision rather than a slight.

verses.text: They had for their inheritance Beersheba (or Sheba), Moladah,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers notice that Beersheba heads the list, a place long tied to the patriarchs’ journeys. Simeon’s towns are woven into the memory of God’s earlier promises to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the naming of towns as a concrete record that God’s promise of land was being fulfilled place by place. Readers in both traditions commonly value the list for what it shows about God’s faithfulness rather than for exact geography.

verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see this short list as a reminder that inheritance is made of real places where families would live, work and worship. The names show that God’s promises touch ordinary life.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see each named town as part of the specific inheritance God gave. Several of these names also appear in Judah’s list and in 1 Chronicles 4, and readers in both traditions commonly hold their exact locations with caution.

verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Hormah, a name tied to earlier struggles in the wilderness, now becomes part of Simeon’s home. Places marked by past conflict can become places of settled life under God’s care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the list continuing as a record of God’s gift, town by town. Readers in both traditions commonly treat these verses as testimony to fulfilled promise rather than as material for doctrinal debate.

verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers notice Ziklag, a town that later plays a part in David’s story. The allotments prepare the stage on which much of Israel’s later history will unfold.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence at work in the allotment of towns whose significance would only become clear later. Both traditions commonly read the list as part of the long story of God’s faithfulness to Israel.

verses.text: Beth Lebaoth, and Sharuhen; thirteen cities with their villages;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the summary of thirteen cities with their villages, showing that each town included its surrounding settlements. Families and communities, not just fortified centers, received their place.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the careful counting as reflecting the orderly way God’s gift was distributed. The way the names add up to thirteen has been explained in more than one way, and readers in both traditions commonly hold such details lightly.

verses.text: Ain, Rimmon, Ether, and Ashan; four cities with their villages;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a second group of four cities added to Simeon’s share, a sign that the tribe’s needs were met. God provides enough for those he places in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the additional towns as part of the same gracious allotment. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that God’s provision extends to the villages around each city.

verses.text: and all the villages that were around these cities to Baalath Beer, Ramah of the South. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Simeon according to their families.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the inheritance extends to Baalath Beer, Ramah of the South, defining the reach of Simeon’s portion. The summary formula affirms that this is truly Simeon’s inheritance by families.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the closing formula as confirming the completeness of God’s gift to this tribe. Both traditions commonly see the repeated phrase according to their families as stressing that the inheritance belonged to real households.

verses.text: Out of the part of the children of Judah was the inheritance of the children of Simeon; for the portion of the children of Judah was too much for them. Therefore the children of Simeon had inheritance in the middle of their inheritance.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Simeon receiving land from Judah’s portion because Judah’s share was too much for them, a picture of a larger tribe making room for a smaller one. Generosity and practicality work together.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in this arrangement God fulfilling Jacob’s word that Simeon would be scattered in Israel (Genesis 49:7), while still giving the tribe a home. Readers in both traditions commonly see both judgment remembered and mercy shown in this outcome.
